concept.name: Unit root
concept.definition: A property of a time series whose autoregressive representation has a root equal to one, making it difference-stationary rather than level-stationary: shocks have permanent effects and the series follows a stochastic trend. A unit-root process becomes stationary only after differencing.
concept.intuition: A series with a unit root has no tendency to return to any fixed level; every shock shifts it permanently, like a drunken walk that wanders without an anchor.
concept.mechanics: Detected with unit-root tests such as the augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test, which regresses the change in the series on its lagged level and lagged changes; the null hypothesis is that a unit root exists (series is non-stationary). Rejection supports stationarity. MacKinnon critical values or p-values are used for significance.
concept.formula: ADF regression: Delta y_t = alpha + beta*y_{t-1} + sum_{i=1..k} gamma_i*Delta y_{t-i} + e_t; null hypothesis beta = 0 (unit root present) versus beta < 0 (stationary).
concept.failure_modes: Unit-root tests have low power against near-stationary alternatives and against trend-stationary processes with structural breaks, frequently failing to reject non-stationarity even when it is false (and vice versa). Spurious regressions arise when unit-root series are regressed on each other without cointegration checks.
concept.misconceptions: That failing to reject the ADF null proves a unit root (the test only fails to find evidence against it), and that a trending series must have a unit root (deterministic trends are stationary around the trend).
concept.example: Testing log S&P 500 prices with the ADF test typically fails to reject the unit-root null, while testing daily returns rejects it, consistent with prices being I(1) and returns I(0).
